setup.panel.title: 3 flags
setup.panel.description: No script or build prints them: you find them by reading the files.
setup.panel.wrong: Not that one. Copy it exactly, braces and all.
setup.flag.skill.label: The skill
setup.flag.skill.hint: A skill the project ships with.
setup.flag.skill.help: A skill is a folder with a SKILL.md in it, as the Skills section above shows. This project ships 1: look where that section says skills live, or ask your agent which skills it has. The flag is in that SKILL.md.
setup.flag.module.label: The project instructions
setup.flag.module.hint: What the agent reads first when you start a session in exercises/step2/java.
setup.flag.module.help: It is the file the first section of this unit is about, and there is one at the top of exercises/step2/java. The agent reads it first when a session starts there. Open it yourself and read it from top to bottom: 1 line holds the flag.
setup.flag.package.label: The package instructions
setup.flag.package.hint: The same kind of file, but inside 1 package, so it only applies there.
setup.flag.package.help: It is the same kind of file as in row 2, but further down, inside 1 package of the source code. The agent only reads it when it works on a file in that package. Go through the packages under src/main/java and open the one with its own copy, or ask your agent to list every copy of that file under exercises/step2/java.
workshop.panel.title: Where they land
workshop.panel.description: Paste each flag as a build, an endpoint or a native image hands it over. Each one is leetspeak between curly braces, and the browser checks it here.
workshop.panel.wrong: Not that one. Read the flag straight from the output it came in.
workshop.flag.coverage.label: Coverage floor
workshop.flag.coverage.hint: 90 percent line coverage on the loans module. The web and config layers are left out, and so is the code the last 2 flags ask you to write.
workshop.flag.coverage.help: This is the goal-shaped one, so hand it over as an outcome rather than a test list: 90 percent, mvn verify -Pgraded after every class, no public signature changed. The unit on long runs argues that shape. If you keep correcting the tests that come back, the prompt was fine. The skill from the pre-flight was missing.
workshop.flag.complexity.label: Complexity ceiling
workshop.flag.complexity.hint: No method above a cyclomatic complexity of 10.
workshop.flag.complexity.help: Hand over the ceiling, not a refactor plan, and name the check it runs after each class. The unit on craft is the shape of the fix: every decision in a small method of its own. If your agent keeps splitting the method the wrong way, that boundary belongs in CLAUDE.md rather than in your next 3 messages.
workshop.flag.honest.label: Honest coverage
workshop.flag.honest.hint: 80 percent of mutations caught: tests that can actually fail.
workshop.flag.honest.help: This is the row that does not move when you add tests, and now is the moment to find out why. Coverage is a proxy: 100 percent of the lines can run under tests that assert nothing, and the number stays green. So the build changes the domain in small ways, runs your tests again, and scores how many of those changes your suite caught. Put the goal on that score and ask for the exact fee each case returns. Asking for tests that assert something is a correction you will keep typing, and the patterns unit puts a correction like that in the skill rather than in another message.
workshop.flag.statement.label: Statement endpoint
workshop.flag.statement.hint: Build the method the failing tests describe, then read the code the endpoint returns.
workshop.flag.statement.help: Plan mode, against a spec you did not write. Run mvn test -Pchallenge, have your agent read the failures and plan MemberStatements.forTier before it writes anything, then read the plan back against the test method names one at a time. A plan that answers the first name and skips the fourth is the failure this row exists for. Then start the service and call the endpoint.
workshop.flag.native.label: Native image
workshop.flag.native.hint: Plan a native image of step 2 that keeps its flag resource. A one-shot compiles and comes up empty.
workshop.flag.native.help: Boot's parent pom already carries the native profile, so mvn -Pnative native:compile is the whole build, and it needs a GraalVM JDK as JAVA_HOME or GRAALVM_HOME, plus a C compiler toolchain. Plan mode tells you what an ahead-of-time image leaves behind before you spend the minutes. Spend them 1 time, run the binary, and read what it prints where the flag should be. If it will not start at all, something else is holding its port.
run-sheet.pair.name: 2 jobs, neither waits
run-sheet.description: The capstone in 4 stages: what you hand over at each, the commands that answer, and the flags each one pays out.
run-sheet.preflight.name: Pre-flight
run-sheet.preflight.hand: The project, before the first message.
run-sheet.goal.name: 1 goal, 3 flags
run-sheet.build.name: Build what is missing
run-sheet.build.hand: A plan, against somebody else's tests.
run-sheet.compile.name: Compile it down
run-sheet.compile.hand: An outcome you cannot iterate your way to.
run-sheet.debrief.name: Debrief
run-sheet.debrief.hand: Your own diff, back to the agent.
set-up-first.title: Set up the environment properly first
set-up-first.description: Spend 10 minutes on the project in exercises/step2/java before a single line of the module changes. Note the time you start; the debrief looks at where that time went.
set-up-first.red.label: Run the first verification: run mvn verify -Pgraded 1 time on an untouched version and read the output carefully.
set-up-first.command.label: Record the validation command: have the agent analyse the project and put the command in exercises/step2/java/CLAUDE.md as the official check for this project.
set-up-first.hook.label: Protect the gate: add a hook (in .claude/settings.json or .github/hooks/) that runs before every edit and shell command, and refuses with exit code 2 anything that touches pom.xml, the grading package or the hook's own files. Then ask the agent to lower COVERAGE_FLOOR and check that it is stopped.
set-up-first.gaps.label: Enforce how unclear points are handled: add the ## Gaps rule, so a run pauses straight away at an undecided point instead of the agent picking the most likely option.
set-up-first.skill.label: Anchor the test conventions in a skill: record this project's existing test conventions in a skill, including the use of AssertJ and exactly 1 @ParameterizedTest per table of test cases.
look-at-afternoon.title: Look at the afternoon
look-at-afternoon.description: Once the flags are in. None of these earns one, and none of them is graded; the tick is a bookmark.
look-at-afternoon.audit.label: Point the agent at your own diff and ask for audit.md as a table, then close its worst row and run the graded build again.
look-at-afternoon.count.label: Split the time you noted 4 ways: setting up, waiting on builds, reading diffs, and deciding.
look-at-afternoon.keep.label: Take the correction you typed more than 2 times and write it into the skill, where it arrives before the next mistake.
look-at-afternoon.asked.label: If no run stopped to ask you anything, go back through the diff for the decision it made instead.
steer.title: Steer a running action
steer.description: You do these tasks in the exercises/step2/java folder. Nothing is graded and nothing is submitted. The tick is only a bookmark for your own progress.
steer.escape.label: Stop an action early: ask a question that is too vague and stop it straight away while the agent is still reasoning. Then run git status to verify that no unwanted changes were made.
steer.queue.claude.label: Steer while it runs: ask the same question again, but this time type the clarification while the agent is working. Watch closely on which turn this extra instruction is picked up.
steer.queue.copilot.label: Steer while it runs: ask the same question again with the Copilot agent, and type the clarification while it works. Watch when it is picked up, then try Send Immediately.
steer.gap.label: Record the rule, then test it: add the ## Gaps rule to exercises/step2/java/CLAUDE.md and then ask the agent to calculate the late fee in euros. Check whether the agent pauses and explicitly asks the clarifying question instead of making an assumption itself.
container-map.question: Where does the app run once the agent starts it?
machinery.title: Develop in a dev container
machinery.description: The kata has a dev container in .devcontainer/: the JDK, Maven, Node, Claude Code and Copilot CLI in 1 image.
machinery.open.label: From the kata's root, build and start the dev container. Docker and Node are all you need.
machinery.agent.claude.label: Start Claude Code inside the container and log in once. The login survives a rebuild.
machinery.agent.copilot.label: Start Copilot CLI inside the container and log in once with /login. Trust the folder and let it save the login when it asks; it survives a rebuild.
machinery.run.label: Ask it to start step 1's service and count the titles it serves. It runs mvn spring-boot:run and curl in the same container.
machinery.run.command: Start step 1's service in the background, then tell me how many titles /api/titles returns.
machinery.view.label: Ask it to start the frontend too, then open localhost:5174/catalog on your laptop and fetch the titles. Your browser reaches the frontend in the container, and the frontend reaches the service.
machinery.view.command: Start the frontend in front/ in the background with npm run dev -- --host 0.0.0.0.
machinery.same.label: In a second terminal, run that project's build yourself in the container, on the same JDK and the same Maven the agent's service runs on.
machinery.same.command: npx -y @devcontainers/cli@0.89.0 exec --workspace-folder . bash -c "cd exercises/step1/java && mvn verify"
machinery.stop.label: When you are done, stop the container from the kata's root. Your logins and Maven's downloads stay in their volumes for next time.
gate-walk.title: Analyse your own quality gates
gate-walk.description: You do this exercise on your own day-to-day work, not inside the kata's practice environment. Nothing is graded and nothing is submitted. The tick is only a bookmark for yourself.
gate-walk.list.label: Map the checkpoints: list every checkpoint a change has to pass on its way to production, both human reviews and automated steps.
gate-walk.mix.label: Check the mix: hold your list against the kinds of check in this unit, and note which ones your pipeline has and which ones it lacks.
gate-walk.reach.label: Work out the impact of mistakes: for each checkpoint, write down how far a mistake has already got in the chain by the time that particular point catches it.
gate-walk.time.label: Time the automated steps: measure how long the automated checkpoints take and mark which steps the agent can run on its own inside its own iteration.
gate-walk.goal.label: Name the main bottleneck: pick the slowest automated checkpoint the agent cannot run on its own. Write a goal for it: the turnaround time you want and the quality requirements that may not be sacrificed for it.
audit.row.headers.remark: X-Content-Type-Options and X-Frame-Options are set, Content-Security-Policy is not. Fix: add it report-only first, then enforce it.
audit.row.audience.topic: The aud claim on a token
audit.row.audience.remark: The decoder checks the signature and the expiry and never looks at aud, so a token minted for another service in the same realm is accepted. Fix: add an audience validator.
audit.row.errors.remark: The handler puts the exception message in the body. On a constraint violation that prints the column names with it. Fix: log it, return a code.
audit.caption: An example security audit, not a run against this repository.
flow-naive.description: You ask, the agent writes the code inside the project. Nothing is settled between you before it does.
flow-plan.description: You and the agent settle the task between you first, and only then does the agent write the code inside the project.
flow-spec.description: You and the agent settle the task between you first, and the agent then writes the code inside the project, which also holds the spec and the plan the code is built from.
fidelity-ladder.description: A ladder of 5 rungs, from low fidelity at the bottom to high fidelity at the top: discussion, diagrams, wireframes, prototypes and production-ready code. Prototypes are the highlighted rung. A dashed line under production-ready code says nothing below it ships.
fidelity-ladder.discussion.name: Discussion
fidelity-ladder.diagram.name: Diagrams
fidelity-ladder.diagram.note: flows and states, as boxes and arrows
fidelity-ladder.wireframe.name: Wireframes
fidelity-ladder.wireframe.note: boxes on a page, no data
fidelity-ladder.prototype.name: Prototypes
fidelity-ladder.production.name: Production-ready code
flow-defer.description: In this session you and the agent work on the task, and what the agent turns up outside it goes down into findings.md instead of into the work. In a later session you read findings.md, turn it into a spec or a prompt, and hand that to the agent, which changes the code in the project.
flow-audit.description: You ask the agent, the agent writes audit.md, you read it, you hand rows back to the agent, and the agent changes the project, which holds the code and, optionally, a spec. Above the row, an agent audits the changed project again and writes a new version of audit.md. Below it, the changed project also comes back to you: you check the fix and close its row in audit.md.
flow-audit.branch-note: check the fix, close the row
workflow-timeline.naive.name: Naive
workflow-timeline.naive.note: A first version, to find out whether the idea stands up at all.
workflow-timeline.plan-first.name: Plan-based
workflow-timeline.plan-first.note: It stood up, so every change gets planned before it is written.
workflow-timeline.specs.name: Spec-driven
workflow-timeline.specs.note: The features that are staying get a spec each, scope and all.
workflow-timeline.audit.name: Audit-driven
workflow-timeline.audit.note: A reflection on what you built, read against what the specs asked for.
workflow-timeline.plan-fixes.name: Plan/naive
workflow-timeline.plan-fixes.note: 1 row of the audit at a time. The small ones you fix straight away, the rest you plan.
workflow-timeline.return: what changed goes back into the specs
workflow-weights.description: 4 bars of the same length, one per workflow, each cut into what you decide first, what the agent runs, and what you read afterwards. Naive decides almost nothing up front and leaves a long read; spec-driven is the reverse.
loops-per-hour.description: How often can the agent prove in 1 hour that its change works? Not running it locally, a push, a pipeline and a deploy to a test environment sit between the change and the proof: 18 minutes in between per try, and 2 proofs in the hour. Running it locally only a restart sits in between: 1 minute, and 10 proofs in the hour.
loops-per-hour.question: How often can the agent prove in 1 hour that its change works?
agents-at-once.description: 4 arrangements drawn as wires from you to the agents you are running. 1 agent on a single solid teal wire. Then 4 agents on 4 thin dashed ones, none of them teal. Then a dashed wire to a pair of agents joined by a wire that runs both ways. Then 1 teal wire to an agent in front, with 3 dashed wires to agents running behind it.
agents-at-once.one.name: 1 agent
agents-at-once.many.name: 4 at once
agents-at-once.recursive.name: A pair, arguing
agents-at-once.mixed.name: 1 in front, 3 behind
script-runs.description: The same request, resetting the database before a demo, run 3 times and drawn 2 times. Each run is a card whose 3 bars are the steps of the reset (dropped, seeded, checked), and a bar's length is how much that step did on that run. Asked in words, the 3 runs come out different. As 1 script, the 3 runs are identical.
script-runs.request: The request, every run: reset the database before a demo
script-runs.legend: bar length: how much that step did on that run
script.title: Record repeated instructions 1 time
script.description: Look for an instruction you have given an agent more than 2 times this week. If nothing comes to mind, use starting and checking the application from this step.
script.name.label: Identify the repetition: name a recurring command or process. You have already run a concrete example: mvn spring-boot:run in the exercises/step2/java folder, followed by curl -s localhost:8082/api/loans/statement/STUDENT | jq to inspect the result.
script.ask.label: Have a script generated: ask the agent to write an automated script for it. Leave the choice of programming language to the agent.
script.twice.label: Track down variation: run the script 2 times and compare the results. Every difference points to free interpretation still locked inside the script.
script.skill.label: Create a skill: create a skill and add a short 1-line description that says when the agent should use it.
script.find.label: Test that it works: start a clean session and ask in your own words for the task to be done. If the agent selects and runs the right script on its own, the description is sharp enough.
two-windows.description: 2 contexts side by side. In the left one the wrong file sits in full, with your correction under it and the next turn after that, and all of it is re-sent on every turn. In the right one you rewound to your request in the same session: the request and the wrong file it led to are struck through as dropped, and the context goes on with the rewritten request and the work, so the wrong turn is never sent again.
two-windows.forward.name: Send a correction
two-windows.forward.note: all of it, re-sent every turn
two-windows.rewind.name: Rewind, in the same session
loop-in-window.description: 2 contexts side by side. The left one holds 4 failed fixes and a 5th coming out the same shape, because the failures are the strongest pattern in the context. The right one is a fresh context holding 1 block you passed on, what did not work and why, and a fresh attempt with room around it.
loop-in-window.dirty.name: The 5th try
loop-in-window.dirty.note: the loop is in the context
loop-in-window.clean.name: The second try
loop-in-window.carried: what did not work, and why
worktree-each.description: One codebase, ~/kata on main. git worktree add makes 2 separate folders beside it, ~/kata-loan-statement on feat/loan-statement with agent 1 and ~/kata-native-image on feat/native-image with agent 2. A third agent merges main into each branch and opens a pull request for each, and ~/kata on main ends up with both changes.
worktree-each.title: How do 2 agents work on 1 codebase at once?
steering-moves.title: What do you do when the agent goes the wrong way?
steering-moves.description: 4 rows, from light to heavy. Something small: type it in while it works, and everything stays, plus your sentence. A wrong direction with usable work: stop it and send a correction, and everything stays, plus your correction. A wrong direction caused by your own request: go back and rewrite the request, and everything up to the request stays. Still not what you wanted after a few attempts: stop and start a new session, and only what you pass on stays.
steering-moves.small.move.claude: type it in while it works
steering-moves.small.move.copilot: type it in while it works
steering-moves.correct.problem.2: the work so far is usable
steering-moves.correct.move.claude: stop it and send a correction
steering-moves.correct.move.copilot: stop it and send a correction
steering-moves.correct.how.copilot: Send Immediately, or the Stop button
steering-moves.restart.move.claude: stop and start a new session
steering-moves.restart.move.copilot: stop and start a new chat
steering-moves.restart.how.claude: say what did not work and why
steering-moves.restart.how.copilot: say what did not work and why
gap-rule.title: What does the agent do when nothing decides it?
gap-rule.description: 2 rows. Without the rule the agent picks a currency itself, builds on it, and you see it at review. With the rule it stops, asks you, and records your answer.
window-spend.description: Illustrative usage within a subscription allowance period, not context capacity. Ordinary work and prepared useful work share the allowance; independent limits still apply.
goal-gate.description: 3 boxes in a row. The agent changes the code, and a dot goes to a box holding the command mvn verify. Twice it comes back red along the path underneath and the agent tries again; the 3rd time it is green and goes on to the box where the run reports back.
read-each-time.description: What each agent is holding. On the left, 1 agent with 3 blocks of reading and 5 pieces of work under them. On the right, 5 agents, each holding an identical copy of those same 3 blocks in front of its 1 piece of work.
model-relay.description: 3 columns joined by 2 teal arrows. A large block of broad research on Fable, a smaller block of planning on Opus, then 5 small blocks of work on Sonnet.
tree.claude-md.note: read at the start of every session
tree.settings.note: permissions, and where hooks are declared
tree.scripts.note: a script, read only when needed
tree.nested-claude-md.note: read only when the agent works in here
tree.module-claude-md.note: the conventions of that module only
tree.rule.note: read only with a file that matches
tree.nested-agents-md.note: in IntelliJ only once nested files are ticked
tree.github-hooks.note: the hook files and the scripts they run
domain-tree.root-pom.note: lists the modules, builds none of them itself
domain-tree.module-pom.note: builds and tests on its own
domain-tree.host.note: the only app, and all it does is assemble the modules
domain-tree.domain.note: the rules, with no dependencies at all
domain-tree.repository-port.note: a port, owned by the use cases
domain-tree.application.note: 1 class per use case, plus the ports it uses
domain-tree.adapter.note: the outside world, and only here
domain-tree.outgoing.note: what the use cases call out to
domain-tree.controller.note: calls the use case, never the aggregate
domain-tree.changelog.note: its own tables, and no other module touches them
domain-tree.test.note: tests mirror the package they cover
domain-tree.caption: An example project, not one in this repository.
spec-tree.root.note: a folder in the repository, or a repository of its own
spec-tree.plan.note: numbered steps, each with its test
spec-tree.caption: An example, not a folder in this repository.
vertical-slices.description: 3 grey horizontal bands: presentation, business logic and data access. Over them 3 teal vertical columns, each 1 use case running through all 3 bands: Record a payment and Refund a payment under a bracket labelled payments, Send an invoice under invoicing. The first 2 carry a check mark and "runs end to end"; the third is lighter and labelled "being built".
vertical-slices.note: every slice is a full loop: build it, run it, check it
slice-skills.description: A T-shape built from labelled cells. Across the top, under the label enough of everything 1 slice touches, 7 cells: Frontend, CI/CD, Cloud, Backend, Ops, Security, AI and ML. Backend is muted, the other 6 are teal. Under Backend hangs a stem of 4 muted cells, Java, Spring, SQL and JPA, API design, labelled your specialism.
words-to-files.description: A prompt reading validate the IBAN on every payment, with the word IBAN picked out. 1 arrow leads from it to payments/Iban.java, the first of 3 files in the repository. The other 2, payments/Payment.java and invoicing/Invoice.java, have nothing pointing at them.
hexagon-ports.description: 2 hexagons, one inside the other: application/, the imperative shell, around domain/, the functional core. Every arrow points inward. On the left 3 adapter boxes call a port on the outer hexagon's edge; on the right 3 adapter boxes implement a port on that edge.
same-gate.description: 2 labels, you write and an agent writes, on lines that join into one before they reach a single box holding 4 rows: tests; coverage and mutation; static analysis and complexity; vulnerabilities and secrets. 1 arrow leaves that box, to ship.
gate-reach.description: 4 gates a change from an agent passes, left to right, with an arrow between each: after every change (tests), when the agent is done (mvn verify), before the merge (CI) and before the release. 3 rows under them. What runs there: unit tests, consumer pacts and architecture rules after every change; integration, coverage and mutation, static rules and secrets when the agent is done; Sonar, the CVE scan, provider pacts and your review before the merge; a person deciding before the release. The answer comes after seconds, 1 minute, minutes or days. A mistake is already in 1 file, your change, a pull request or main, in cells that darken to the right. An arrow under them: the further left, the sooner the agent finds its own mistake.
gate-reach.gate.loop.name: after every change
gate-reach.gate.done.name: when the agent is done
gate-reach.gate.merge.name: before the merge
gate-reach.gate.release.name: before the release
gate-reach.note: The further left, the sooner the agent finds its own mistake.
quiz.small-change-no-spec.question: Your team has agreed to keep a spec file for every feature. Today's plan holds only moving a log line and making a column optional. Writing the specs takes considerably longer than making the changes themselves. Which approach is most effective here?
quiz.small-change-no-spec.nudge: Make the changes straight in the code. A minimal change that calls for no architectural decisions does not need a heavy procedure.
quiz.small-change-no-spec.consistency: Write the specs as agreed. A process that is only followed for big changes loses its value as a quality standard.
quiz.small-change-no-spec.batch: Collect several small changes until together they fit in 1 overarching spec file, to keep the documentation tidy.
quiz.small-change-no-spec.audit: Make the changes straight away and then run a check over the whole repository to catch any side effects.
quiz.small-change-no-spec.explanation: A spec is worth writing when something is being decided. A log line and a nullable column decide nothing, so the spec is cost with no answer in it.
quiz.plan-mode-interview.question: Instead of asking for code changes straight away, you now ask the agent for a step-by-step plan first. The final quality of the code is noticeably higher. That surprises you, since you approve most plans without major changes. Where does the main gain of this approach lie?
quiz.plan-mode-interview.interview: Drawing up the plan forces a conversation in which overlooked constraints become clear before the first line of code is written.
quiz.plan-mode-interview.thinking: The model goes through an extra reasoning step before it generates the code, which shows up as a stronger first draft.
quiz.plan-mode-interview.document: The plan stays in the repository, so a follow-up session builds straight on the decisions that were made.
quiz.plan-mode-interview.review: Reviewing a written plan takes less time than reading a diff, so you spot any flawed reasoning sooner.
quiz.plan-mode-interview.explanation: You approve most plans because answering the questions was the work. The agent asks how many days late a member can be before the fee starts and what happens when the list comes back empty, and the workflow puts you back in the design.
quiz.audit-as-essay.question: You ask an agent whether a specific module is complete and secure and whether it fits the architecture of the rest of the repository. The agent delivers 4 pages of extensive text. You read the analysis and mostly agree with it. A week later, though, it is unclear which points were actually dealt with. What is the main cause of this problem?
quiz.audit-as-essay.format: No structured format was asked for. A clear table forces concrete action points and stays in the repository for reference.
quiz.audit-as-essay.scope: 3 different aspects were combined in 1 question. Splitting completeness, security and style into separate analyses keeps the advice manageable.
quiz.audit-as-essay.memory: The analysis was lost when the session closed. Adding the report back at the start of a new session lets you pick up the thread again.
quiz.audit-as-essay.model: Extensive prose is a sign that the agent is unsure of the outcome. A more specific question gets a more focused, shorter answer.
quiz.audit-as-essay.explanation: An audit is a file in your repository, so it diffs and gets reviewed the way the code does. Ask for the topic, where it lives, how solid it is and what to do about it, and you have rows to work rather than paragraphs to re-read.
quiz.report-on-a-wish.question: You ask an agent to clean up an old module, with only the instruction to refine the code and keep the tests passing. After 4 hours and a sizeable amount of compute, the agent reports the task is done. The diff is huge, yet the structure has barely changed. What went wrong?
quiz.report-on-a-wish.no-command: No hard end criterion was defined. Passing tests say what may not break, but not when the work is done.
quiz.report-on-a-wish.too-long: The run took too long. Split into 4 separate 1-hour goals, it would have kept its focus.
quiz.report-on-a-wish.wrong-tier: The chosen model did not suit the task. Restructuring code calls for judgement, which on a simpler model leads to needless rewriting.
quiz.report-on-a-wish.no-worktree: The agent worked on your active branch. Changes made in the meantime kept it rereading files and it lost the overview.
quiz.report-on-a-wish.explanation: A goal is a task with an outcome something else can measure, and "cleaner" is not one. Name the command that prints the answer, a coverage floor or a complexity ceiling, and the run has something to run until.
quiz.fleet-bill.question: You start 5 fresh workers with the same background files. The usage report shows those files processed separately by each worker. Why can that cost more than a sequential session?
quiz.fleet-bill.read-again: The workers each process shared background context; cache rates can reduce that cost but do not remove it.
quiz.fleet-bill.overwrote: The agents worked in the same files at the same time, so a sizeable part of the work was done 2 times.
quiz.fleet-bill.gathered: The results of all the agents were merged into 1 context at the end, so that whole report is loaded again with every following turn.
quiz.fleet-bill.pricier-tier: A set-up with several agents runs on the top model by default, since simpler models cannot carry the coordination.
quiz.fleet-bill.explanation: These fresh workers duplicate background processing across requests. The extra usage buys parallel progress; inherited context and caching depend on configuration.
quiz.window-tail.question: Your allowance period ends soon and you have used only half of it. What do you do with the rest?
quiz.window-tail.spend-it: Start prepared work that is worth doing, if your other limits and budget allow it.
quiz.window-tail.save-it: Leave it. What you do not use carries over to the next period.
quiz.window-tail.keep-busy: Give the agent any task that keeps it busy, so the capacity is not wasted.
quiz.window-tail.upgrade-small: Move small tasks to the most expensive model, since the capacity is paid for anyway.
quiz.window-tail.explanation: Unused allowance does not carry over, but spending it is only worth something when the work is. A reset does not lift your other limits either, such as a weekly limit or a budget your admin set.
quiz.wrong-turn-nothing-written.question: Your question could be read 2 ways and the agent opened the wrong file. No code has been written or changed yet. What is the right next step?
quiz.wrong-turn-nothing-written.rewind: Go back to your original question, rephrase it and let the agent start again.
quiz.wrong-turn-nothing-written.correct-: Send a correction straight away that names the right file explicitly.
quiz.wrong-turn-nothing-written.clear: Stop the run, clear the session history and start completely from scratch.
quiz.wrong-turn-nothing-written.queue: Have the correction ready in the input box so the agent picks it up on the next turn.
quiz.wrong-turn-nothing-written.explanat: Nothing has been written, so a rewind costs nothing and takes the wrong turn out of the context. A correction leaves the wrong file in the context for the rest of the session.
quiz.third-correction.question: Over the week you have told the agent 3 times not to put a closing summary at the bottom of a file. The agent applies the correction straight away, but on the next file the summary appears again. What causes this recurring behaviour?
quiz.third-correction.no-home: The correction only lives in the active session and is not kept for future sessions.
quiz.third-correction.context-full: The amount of information in the context has grown too large, so the instruction has dropped out of memory.
quiz.third-correction.wrong-model: The chosen model's capacity is too limited to hold on to a specific instruction of this kind.
quiz.third-correction.prompt-wording: The instruction is worded too generally and needs a more specific scope.
quiz.third-correction.explanation: A correction you repeat is knowledge with no home yet. Written into a skill it is a file in the repository, so every later session can load it when the task matches.
quiz.skill-still-off.question: The skill for generating commit messages works as intended, but it keeps going wrong on 1 specific detail. You have just corrected the commit message by hand. What is the most effective next step to make this improvement stick?
quiz.skill-still-off.both-versions: Show the agent both the generated version and your corrected version, and have it work out which instruction is missing from the skill.
quiz.skill-still-off.longer-prompt: Put the missing rule in your next message, so the agent can apply it straight away.
quiz.skill-still-off.stricter-descriptio: Change the skill's description so the agent triggers it sooner.
quiz.skill-still-off.rewrite-skill: Rewrite the whole skill from scratch, since a recurring mistake points to the wrong set-up.
quiz.skill-still-off.explanation: The repair is the rule the skill is missing, and the agent can name it from the 2 versions. Writing that answer back is the pass that makes the skill sound like you.
quiz.script-or-skill.question: Before every demo you reset the database, add 3 test users and start the application. Each time you explain this sequence to the agent again. Every run produces small differences in the data. Which approach guarantees a predictable, reusable way of working?
quiz.script-or-skill.script-and-skill: Writing an automated script that carries out the steps, combined with a skill that calls the script when it is needed.
quiz.script-or-skill.longer-skill: A skill with every step written out as text, since the agent can run the commands on its own.
quiz.script-or-skill.claude-md: Adding an instruction to CLAUDE.md, so the steps are loaded again on every interaction.
quiz.script-or-skill.plan-mode: Having the agent draw up a step-by-step plan, after which it follows its own documentation from then on.
quiz.script-or-skill.explanation: Steps that must end in the same state every time belong in a script. The skill beside it is only what makes the agent aware the script is there.
quiz.deep-not-wide.question: Your afternoon is clear. For a new feature you want to work out which classes the domain gets and where the late-fee calculation belongs. Nothing about it is written down yet. Which set-up do you pick?
quiz.deep-not-wide.one-agent: 1 agent in 1 session, and you read every step as it works.
quiz.deep-not-wide.four-drafts: 4 agents that each work out their own domain model, and you pick the best design.
quiz.deep-not-wide.front-and-behind: 1 agent in front on the model, and 3 behind it writing the tests for it.
quiz.deep-not-wide.orchestrated: 1 agent that splits up the design and hands the pieces to sub-agents.
quiz.deep-not-wide.explanation: Here the decision is the work, and you make it in a conversation you follow step by step. Agents in the background cannot start on a model that is not settled yet.
quiz.green-and-unread.question: 4 agents worked all afternoon at once on 4 modules, each in its own worktree. All the tests are green. Of the 4 diffs, you have read 2 carefully. What is going on here?
quiz.green-and-unread.reading-at-the-end: The steering you skipped along the way comes back now as reading, and the last diff gets less attention than the first.
quiz.green-and-unread.builds-are-the-che: It all went well: the tests are the quality check, and they are all green.
quiz.green-and-unread.window-too-small: The agents lost quality for lack of context, so their later work is weaker than the start.
quiz.green-and-unread.shared-branch: The agents should have worked on 1 branch, so everything would have been merged along the way.
quiz.green-and-unread.explanation: With 4 at once you stop steering and only receive results. Green tests say the checks passed, not that the code is what you wanted, and your attention runs out long before your tokens do.
quiz.fifth-fix-same-shape.question: After 4 attempts in a row the test still fails in exactly the same way. The agent's latest change undoes the previous fix. What do you do now?
quiz.fifth-fix-same-shape.clear-and-carr: Stop the run, clear the session and start again with only the error message and a summary of the approach that did not work.
quiz.fifth-fix-same-shape.rewind: Go back to the first message the session started with and rewrite that opening question.
quiz.fifth-fix-same-shape.tell-it: Tell the agent the last 4 attempts got nowhere and ask it to try an alternative route.
quiz.fifth-fix-same-shape.paste-output: Paste the output of the failing test into the context again and let the agent carry on.
quiz.fifth-fix-same-shape.explanation: Repeated failed approaches can keep steering the next attempt. A fresh session removes that task history so you can restart with the current files and a better brief.
quiz.logged-and-carried-on.question: CLAUDE.md holds the standing rule for handling unclear points. The agent delivers a diff and lists 3 assumptions at the bottom of its summary. What went wrong here?
quiz.logged-and-carried-on.should-have-s: The agent should have stopped straight away and asked for clarification. The proposed diff is now built on assumptions.
quiz.logged-and-carried-on.nothing-wrong: Nothing. The agent followed the rule properly and listed its assumptions neatly.
quiz.logged-and-carried-on.wrong-place: This rule belongs in the instructions to the agent, not in CLAUDE.md.
quiz.logged-and-carried-on.commit-messag: The assumptions belong in the commit message, so the reviewer can read them right next to the code.
quiz.logged-and-carried-on.explanation: Write an assumption down and build on it anyway, and you get a list of guesses under a diff that already depends on them. Stopping is the part of the rule that matters.
quiz.pair-buys-rounds.question: You are in meetings all afternoon. Before you go, you put a builder and a critic on a change, with a limit of 3 rounds. What do you have when you get back?
quiz.pair-buys-rounds.rounds-you-skip: A diff that has been through up to 3 review rounds you would otherwise have done yourself, and that you still read.
quiz.pair-buys-rounds.two-are-faster: The change sooner than 1 agent would make it, because the 2 split the work between them.
quiz.pair-buys-rounds.signed-off: A change you can merge without reading it, because the critic has already approved it.
quiz.pair-buys-rounds.steer-as-it-goes: A list of questions from the critic, waiting for your answer before the builder goes on.
quiz.pair-buys-rounds.explanation: The critic takes over the review rounds you would otherwise do yourself, and that costs tokens instead of your afternoon. It signs nothing off: you read the diff and the open findings yourself.

deck.setup.divider.3: A hook is <hi>the strictest</hi> of the 3
deck.engineering.divider.1: <hi>Structural leverage:</hi> A logical project and folder structure gives an agent much more grip on the code.
deck.engineering.divider.2: <hi>Information compression:</hi> Pattern names and domain terms pack complex logic into a few powerful words.
deck.engineering.divider.3: <hi>Efficient context:</hi> The better the language and structure, the fewer tokens the agent needs to stay on the right course.
deck.gates.divider.1: <hi>The new bottleneck:</hi> The delay is no longer in the writing, but in the moment someone makes the decision.
deck.gates.divider.2: <hi>Built into the run:</hi> Quality gates belong in the automated workflow, not as a checklist in human memory.
deck.gates.divider.3: <hi>Autonomous feedback:</hi> An effective gate is a fast test or check the agent can run and fix by itself.
deck.steering.divider.1: <hi>Stopping costs:</hi> An early stop only costs the changes already physically written to disk.
deck.steering.divider.2: <hi>Correction:</hi> Adds an extra instruction to the stack → grows the context and the noise.
deck.steering.divider.3: <hi>Rewind:</hi> Removes the faulty step from the context entirely → restores the clean state.
deck.steering.divider.4: <hi>Context pollution:</hi> A run that got stuck stays in the context as noise until you physically clean it up.
deck.steering.midflight.title: Pick the move by <hi>what went wrong</hi>
deck.parallel.worktree.title: A worktree each: <hi>separate checkouts</hi>
deck.parallel.worktree.note: 2 agents are 2 contexts and 2 bills, and 2 diffs you did not write.
deck.steering.gaps.title: Make it <hi>stop and ask</hi>
deck.patterns.divider.1: <hi>Spot the repetition:</hi> Typed 3 times = time for a fixed format.
deck.patterns.divider.2: <hi>Close the feedback loop:</hi> Correct the result and fill the gaps in the skill straight away.
deck.patterns.divider.3: <hi>A guaranteed output:</hi> Replace vague LLM generation with the hard predictability of a script.
deck.workflows.divider.1: <hi>The continuum:</hi> Naive → Plan → Spec → Audit (from minimal framing up front to maximal specification).
deck.workflows.divider.2: <hi>Dynamic choice:</hi> Decide the approach per individual task, not for a whole project at once.
deck.workflows.divider.3: <hi>Lifespan as the measure:</hi> Let the expected lifespan of the code decide how much specification you need up front.
deck.parallel.divider.1: <hi>Attention & grip:</hi> 1 agent gives maximum control; 4 agents at once split your attention down to a quarter.
deck.parallel.divider.2: <hi>Autonomous loops:</hi> Patterns such as Builder + Critic run their own refinement loop without human intervention.
deck.parallel.divider.3: <hi>Daily practice:</hi> Mostly work with 1 active agent up front and let the rest run in the background.
deck.goals.divider.1: <hi>Outcome-driven prompting:</hi> Define the end result you want (the outcome), not the individual steps or keystrokes.
deck.goals.divider.2: <hi>Binary testing:</hi> Make the quality check an automated command that returns a hard yes or no.
deck.goals.divider.3: <hi>Budget & limits:</hi> Plan only valuable work that can be finished within the set time and token limits.
deck.goals.divider.4: <hi>Isolated execution:</hi> Run long tasks (e.g. 4 hours) in their own git worktree, so you can keep working undisturbed.

access.title: Test a permission
access.description: Everything happens in a practice folder with dummy files, outside your projects. Nothing else changes.
access.prepare.label: Make the practice folder with 2 dummy files.
access.prepare.command: mkdir ~/permission-practice && cd ~/permission-practice && echo "dummy allowed" > allowed.txt && echo "dummy blocked" > blocked.txt
access.restrict.claude.label: Add a .claude/settings.json that denies reading blocked.txt and allows touch.
access.start.claude.label: Start Claude Code there and say yes when it asks whether you trust the folder. An allow rule in the project's settings only counts in a folder you trust.
access.start.copilot.label: Start Copilot CLI there with a deny on reading blocked.txt and an allow on touch. Say yes when it asks whether you trust this folder.
access.test.label: Give it this task. Reading blocked.txt is refused, touch runs without asking, and cp asks first: decline.
access.test.command: read blocked.txt, then run touch made-by-agent.txt and cp allowed.txt copy.txt
access.explain.claude.label: Now ask it to read blocked.txt with a Node script. Your rule does not cover that route. The agent often refuses on its own, and otherwise Claude Code asks you first: decline. Either way, a judgement stopped it and not your rule.
access.explain.copilot.label: Now have it print blocked.txt with head. That works: the rule covers the read tool, not the shell.
access.explain.copilot.command: print blocked.txt by running head blocked.txt
access.clean.label: Exit the agent and delete the practice folder.
